walkthrough.lead: Start to finish, here's the whole thing.
walkthrough.shot_s1: Reporting a fault at the machine — scan the code, rate the condition, attach a photo.
walkthrough.shot_s2: Approving the request. The status change is saved to the history with its note.

resources.check_desc: What to gather before a first site goes live. Seven items, in the order they matter.

equip.title: Equipment health
equip.d1: The share of a period the machine was usable. This is the one production understands, because it answers “was the machine there when I needed it?”
equip.d2: Mean time between failures: running time divided by the number of failures. It measures the equipment's reliability, not how fast you repair it.
equip.d3: Mean time to repair: total repair time divided by the number of repairs. It measures your responsiveness — part availability, technician availability, documentation.
equip.d4: The total hours the machine was not usable. Worth splitting between planned and unplanned: the two do not cost the same.
equip.d5: Failures expressed against 1,000 running hours. It lets you compare two machines that do not run the same number of hours.
equip.d6: An aggregate score per machine, built from the measures above. Useful for ranking a fleet, not for diagnosing one machine.

stock.title: Parts inventory
stock.d1: The total value of parts held, at catalogue prices. This is the capital sitting on the shelves.
stock.d2: How many times an item is consumed and replenished over a period. Low turnover marks stock that is sleeping.
stock.d3: Items with no movement over a given period. These are the first candidates for a review of minimum levels.
stock.d4: The gap between the level on screen and the level counted in a physical inventory. Below a certain threshold the numbers stop being usable.
stock.d5: How often a requested item was not available. Every stockout lengthens the MTTR of the job that needed it.
stock.d6: The time between placing an order and receiving it. This is what determines the minimum level an item has to hold.

check.d1: Every machine with its model, serial number, location, department and criticality. It is the only thing genuinely required on day one — everything else attaches to it.
check.d2: Where the QR codes go, and who applies them. This is the physical part, the one that takes real time on the floor, and the one that makes reporting possible without an account.
check.d3: The items to track, their stores and locations, and a minimum level for each. The minimum is set from the supplier lead time, not from instinct.
check.d4: Who is a manager, who is a technician, who is a requester. Operators reporting by QR code need no account, so they need no entry here.
check.d5: What is already done on a routine, and on what trigger: a date, a meter, or both. Bring them across as they are — the history will say later what should change.
check.d6: The spreadsheets and notebooks in use. We bring across the equipment and the parts; past history can stay archived rather than be retyped.
check.d7: Currency, timezone, date format and organisation language. The defaults are dirham, Africa/Casablanca, DD/MM/YYYY, French or English.

hero.lead: Two records, on purpose. A request is what somebody saw. A work order is what the team agreed to do about it. Keeping them apart stops a passing remark from turning into an unplanned intervention.

benefits.b1_title: Anyone on site can raise a request
benefits.b1_body: Scanning the QR code on a machine opens the form: equipment, criticality, description, photo. Operators do not need an account, so faults get reported when they are seen.
benefits.b2_body: Requests queue as pending, approved, refused or flagged to schedule. Approving one turns it into a work order and links the two records together.
benefits.b3_body: A work order carries its own steps, from isolation and lockout through diagnosis, repair and return to service. Checklists can require a yes or no answer and a comment before the job closes.
benefits.b4_title: Hours and parts recorded as they happen
benefits.b4_body: The technician logs time against the job and the parts pulled from the store. The stock movement is written at the same moment, so the shelf and the system agree.

flow.title: The states a job passes through
flow.s1_desc: Created against a machine with a criticality and a description. Reference in the DI-2026-###### series.
flow.s2_desc: Approved, refused, or flagged as an intervention to schedule. The decision keeps the reviewer's name.
flow.s3_desc: Sub-tasks, checklists, assigned technician and due date. Reference in the OT series.
flow.s4_desc: Hours logged, parts consumed, PDF produced, machine availability updated.

cta.title: See a request become a work order

hero.lead: Set the plan once. MainteNeat writes the work order when the date arrives or the counter passes its threshold, with the task template and equipment already attached.

benefits.b1_body: A plan runs on a frequency in days, weeks or months, on a meter reading such as 4,000 running hours, or on whichever of the two comes first.
benefits.b2_title: The work order appears before it is due
benefits.b2_body: You choose how many days ahead the job is created, so parts can be pulled and a technician booked before the machine is due to stop.
benefits.b3_body: A plan can count its next run from the day the last job actually closed instead of the day it was created. A service done a week late moves the whole cycle with it.
benefits.b4_body: The steps for a given service are written once as a template and reused by every plan that needs them. Changing the template changes the jobs that have not opened yet.

detail.title: What triggers a plan
detail.lead: A preventive plan is set once. Its trigger rules decide when it writes its work order.
detail.d1: A period: monthly, quarterly. The simplest, and the right choice when wear follows time rather than use.
detail.d2: A threshold on a reading — running hours, cycles, kilometres. A machine that is barely used is not serviced for nothing.
detail.d3: Whichever comes first triggers it. This is the rule for equipment whose wear depends on use without being independent of time.
detail.d4: The work order is created N days before it is due, so the part can be drawn and the slot booked.
detail.d5: The next cycle counts from the date the job actually closed, not from when it was created. A monthly plan that slipped three weeks does not ask for the same job again three weeks later.

hero.lead: Spare parts tied to the jobs that consume them. Levels drop when a technician logs a part, and a purchase order starts when an item falls under its minimum.

benefits.b1_body: Parts live in named stores broken into locations, so a technician is told where to go instead of which shelf to search.
benefits.b2_body: Every consumption, issue and receipt is a movement with its own reference and date. The level is the result of those movements, which is why it can be trusted.
benefits.b3_title: Alerts before the shelf is empty
benefits.b3_body: Items show as in stock, low, or out of stock against the minimum you set. The reports flag dormant stock and inventory accuracy as well.
benefits.b4_body: Purchase orders, supplier records and the outside firms you send work to, held with the parts and jobs they relate to.

cta.title: Stop keeping parts in a spreadsheet

detail.title: The four stock movements
detail.lead: Every change in level carries a type and its own reference. That is what lets you answer “where did that part go” without reconstructing it.
detail.d1: A part logged against a job. The level drops when the technician records it, not at the end of the month.
detail.d2: A part leaving the store without being attached to a job — a loan, or a transfer between locations.
detail.d3: An incoming supplier delivery. It reconciles the quantity received against the purchase order that triggered it.
detail.d4: The count on site. The gap against the level on screen gives you inventory accuracy, and corrects the stock.

hero.lead: Every machine with its model, serial number, location, department, criticality and the whole history of what has been done to it. Each one carries a QR code that opens its record on a phone.

criticality.title: Criticality sets the priority
criticality.lead: The level on a machine decides where its faults sit in the queue and how quickly a failure escalates.

benefits.b1_body: Model, serial number, acquisition date, supplier, department and location. Sub-equipment hangs off the parent, so a line and its components stay related.
benefits.b2_title: A QR code on the machine
benefits.b2_body: Scanning it opens the equipment record. From there anyone can raise a request without an account, and signed-in users can open a work order or enter a meter reading.
benefits.b3_body: Online, offline and untracked periods are recorded per machine, with planned and unplanned stops separated. That history is where availability and MTBF come from.

cta.title: Put your machine list in one place

hero.lead: Four report views built from work the team has already done: jobs, equipment health, maintenance cost and parts inventory. Nothing is typed in twice.

categories.title: Four views
categories.lead: Pick one to see what it covers.
categories.cat1_desc: How much is open, how fast it moves, and whether jobs close inside their window.
categories.cat1_kpi1_body: The current split across states, so the size of the backlog is visible without counting anything.
categories.cat1_kpi2_body: How many jobs closed inside their target window. A steady share of late jobs means the planning is not realistic.
categories.cat1_kpi3_body: Low, medium, high and urgent side by side. A queue that is mostly urgent is a queue nobody is planning.
categories.cat1_kpi4_body: The balance between planned work and reaction. Moving this ratio is the point of a preventive programme.
categories.cat1_kpi5_body: What operators have reported and nobody has looked at yet.
categories.cat2_desc: Which machines are reliable and which are quietly eating production time.
categories.cat2_kpi1_body: The share of scheduled running time a machine was actually online, taken from its status history.
categories.cat2_kpi2_body: Mean time between failures. Falling MTBF on an ageing machine is the argument for replacing it.
categories.cat2_kpi3_body: Mean time to repair, from opening to closing. Rising MTTR means jobs are getting harder or the team is stretched.
categories.cat2_kpi4_body: Failures per 1,000 running hours, so machines of different ages and duty cycles can be compared.
categories.cat2_kpi5_body: A single figure across the fleet, useful for spotting a direction of travel between reviews.
categories.cat3_desc: Where the budget goes, by job and by machine, in dirhams.
categories.cat3_kpi1_body: Labour and parts on each closed job. A rising average points at ageing equipment, or at work being done twice.
categories.cat3_kpi2_body: Total spend on one machine over a period, which is the number a replacement decision needs.
categories.cat3_kpi3_body: The split between materials and technician hours, useful when negotiating supply contracts or headcount.
categories.cat3_kpi4_body: What was bought next to what was used, month by month. A widening gap means stock is building up.
categories.cat3_kpi5_body: The monthly trend, so an unusual month is visible while you can still ask why.
categories.cat4_desc: What is on the shelf, what it is worth, and whether the records match reality.
categories.cat4_kpi1_body: The value held across every store, in dirhams, with the split per store.
categories.cat4_kpi2_body: How quickly parts are used and replaced. Very low turnover means capital sitting in parts nobody fits.
categories.cat4_kpi3_body: Value that has not moved in a year, reported separately because it rarely shows up in a headline figure.
categories.cat4_kpi4_body: How closely counted stock matches the system. Low accuracy is why jobs stall on parts the system says exist.
categories.cat4_kpi5_body: How often you ran out, and how long the replacement actually took to arrive.

hero.lead: Preventive plans, scheduled jobs and open work orders on one calendar, in day, week, month or list view, with a workload view per technician.

benefits.b1_title: Unplanned jobs sit next to the calendar
benefits.b1_body: Work orders with no date wait in their own tray. Drag one onto a day to schedule it, and the technician's workload updates with it.
benefits.b2_body: The team view shows how many jobs each person is carrying. Somebody holding four jobs while a colleague holds none is visible before the shift, not after.

detail.title: Four views, one source
detail.lead: Preventive plans, scheduled jobs and open work orders are the same records, looked at from four angles.
detail.d1: What is due today, by technician. This is the morning view, the one used to hand work out.
detail.d2: The load across the next seven days. It shows collisions before they happen — two heavy preventive jobs on the same Thursday.
detail.d3: The planning view. Preventive plans appear on the date they will write their work order.
detail.d4: The same thing without a calendar, filterable and sortable. This is the view you export or print.
detail.d5: One lane per person, plus a tray of unplanned jobs. It answers “who can take this”.

technician.desc: Sees the jobs assigned to them. Works the checklist, logs hours and parts, closes the job and produces the report.

qr.p3: No login and no account needed

cta.title: Give each role the screen it needs

hero.lead: Every status change, approval, assignment and edit is stamped with a time and a name. When an auditor asks what happened to a machine, the answer is a query.

benefits.b1_body: Requests and work orders carry their own history: who moved them, from which state to which, and when. The trail stays with the record.
benefits.b2_title: A PDF on every closed job
benefits.b2_body: Produced at closing with the work done, the technician, hours logged and parts fitted. Ready to file or hand over.
benefits.b3_body: Manuals, certificates and photographs stored on the machine record, so the person holding the spanner has them.
benefits.b4_body: Work orders, equipment, locations and suppliers export on demand. The data is not locked inside the product.

audit.title: What is recorded without anyone doing it
audit.e1_sub: Who raised it, against which machine, from a QR scan or an account, and when.
audit.e2_sub: The decision, the person who made it, and the time it was made.
audit.e3_sub: Which manager assigned it, to which technician, with what due date.
audit.e4_sub: Which parts, how many, from which store, and the stock movement that followed.
audit.e5_sub: Hours logged, closing note, the generated PDF and the availability update on the machine.

signup.description: Signing up starts a setup, not a trial you work through on your own. Tell us about the site and we come back with a quote and a date.

pricing.title: CMMS pricing in dirhams — MainteNeat
pricing.description: One price for the whole company, billed in dirhams. Adding a technician does not change the bill, and there is no licence to buy up front.

comparison.title: CMMS comparison: Excel, ERP or imported tools — MainteNeat
comparison.description: How MainteNeat sits against a spreadsheet, a foreign ERP module, a heavy imported CMMS, and the newer mobile tools.

industries.title: Industries and sites served — MainteNeat
industries.description: The product suits sites with a fixed set of machines and a maintenance team on the payroll. See whether your operation fits.

enterprise.title: Multi-site deployment — MainteNeat
enterprise.description: For groups running several plants, or with IT requirements a standard subscription does not cover.

resources.title: Maintenance resources — MainteNeat
resources.description: Practical material on running maintenance, written for the people doing it: guides, KPI definitions and a setup checklist.

blog.title: Blog — industrial maintenance and CMMS — MainteNeat
blog.description: Articles and insights on maintenance management: CMMS, preventive maintenance, KPIs and notes from the shop floor.

workOrders.title: Requests and work orders — MainteNeat
workOrders.description: Two records, on purpose. A request is what somebody saw. A work order is what the team agreed to do about it.

equipment.title: Equipment and sites — MainteNeat
equipment.description: Every machine with its model, serial number, location, department, criticality and the whole history of what has been done to it.

preventiveMaintenance.title: Preventive maintenance plans — MainteNeat
preventiveMaintenance.description: Set the plan once. MainteNeat writes the work order when the date arrives or the counter passes its threshold, task template included.

inventory.title: Spare parts stock and purchasing — MainteNeat
inventory.description: Spare parts tied to the jobs that consume them. Levels drop when a technician logs a part, and a purchase order starts at the minimum.

kpiDashboard.title: Maintenance reports: MTBF, MTTR, availability — MainteNeat
kpiDashboard.description: Four report views built from work the team has already done: jobs, equipment health, maintenance cost and parts inventory.

maintenanceCalendar.title: Maintenance calendar and field teams — MainteNeat
maintenanceCalendar.description: Preventive plans, scheduled jobs and open work orders on one calendar, in day, week, month or list view, with workload per technician.

reporting.title: Audit trail and documentation — MainteNeat
reporting.description: Every status change, approval, assignment and edit is stamped with a time and a name. Enough to answer an auditor.

roles.title: Roles and access — MainteNeat
roles.description: Three signed-in roles plus a QR route that needs no account. Each one sees the part of the system its job requires.
